titulo: The downside: the bill, and how to manage it
lead: With an agent running all day, usage grows fast: on a subscription you hit the limit; paying per use, it becomes a big bill. In my case, almost everything runs on the subscription. As with any employee, you need to audit and watch the cost. First what applies to everyone: the right model and keeping track of the bill. Then, for those who pay per use, cache and batch.
objetivo: choose the right model for each recurring task, track a week of usage and know when cache and batch are worth it.

aprende.t: The right model for each job
When to send in a batch

hero_alt: Dark desk with an analog meter, a calculator and a notebook; in the background, servers with cool lights.

nos.detalhe: Not every task needs the strongest model. Sorting messages or pulling out a single field goes to the smallest; writing and reviewing goes to the middle one; decisions and what really makes a difference go to the largest. The names, from smallest to largest: in Claude, Haiku → Sonnet → Opus or Fable (Fable is the newest and strongest of them); in ChatGPT, the "mini" versions → the standard model → the reasoning and "Pro" ones; in Gemini, Flash → Pro. You pick the model in the selector at the top of the conversation; what shows up there depends on your plan.

Write down how much each task uses: on a subscription, how many times you hit the limit and with which task; on the API, the dollar amount. A well-trained agent can already handle a good share of your tasks, and the whole team can talk to it in the same channel. If you don't track cost, it only shows up on the bill.

This applies if you pay per use through the API (direct access to the model by program, billed by volume). If you repeat the same start of a conversation (the rules, the profile, the documents) in a short time, that part is saved and costs a fraction of the price. That's why it pays to keep the start fixed and leave what changes for the end.

This one is also an API feature. Whatever can wait (reports, bulk classifications, translations) goes through the API's batch option (sending in bulk), which charges half the price and returns the result within a day. A task someone is waiting on right now stays out of the batch.

secoes.legenda: Audit it the way you would audit an employee: what it delivers, how much it costs and whether the model is the right one for the job.
secoes.dica: In my case, the model for each system is written down in one single place. When a better or cheaper one comes out, I change it on one line, without hunting through the rest.

secoes.sub: Three questions for each recurring task. Tap or click each one.

texto: Simple and repetitive goes to the smallest; everyday text and analysis to the middle one; anything with risk or that decides money to the largest.
If in doubt, run the procedure from lesson 6 on both and compare.

exemplo.texto: Sorting emails by subject: smaller model. Proposal for a client: larger model.

texto: If you only use the chat subscription, cache and batch don't show up for you: the provider takes care of that.
What counts is picking the right model, not repeating the context for nothing (the project already keeps it) and noticing when you hit the limit.

exemplo.texto: Hit the limit every Thursday? See which task used the larger model without needing to.

texto: If nobody is waiting for the answer right now, the task can go in a batch for half the price.
Gather the day's tasks and send them all at once.

exemplo.texto: Weekly summary of 200 customer reviews: batch.

texto: If every call starts with the same rules and documents, keep that start identical and at the beginning.
What changes (the question, the case) goes at the end.

exemplo.texto: Customer service: rules and price table always the same at the start; the customer's message at the end.

blocos.rot: Request: review the cost with the agent itself
blocos.conteudo:
Below is the list of tasks you do for me every week.
For each one, tell me:
1. whether it really needs the larger model, or whether the smaller one can handle it (and how I test that);
2. whether it can wait and go in a batch;
3. whether the start of the request is always the same (and what I keep fixed to take advantage of the cache).
Answer in a table and don't change anything yet.

<list of tasks>

abas.html:
• Sorting emails by topic · 50×/week · smaller · on the spot · fixed start.
  • Review summary · 1×/week · middle · batch.
  • Client proposal · 3×/week · larger · on the spot.

Decision: the summary goes to batch; the email sorting drops to the smaller model after it passes the 5-round test.

• Everything on the larger model "just to be safe": you pay a lot for what the smaller one does just as well.
  • Switching models without testing: run the procedure on both and compare.
  • Changing the start of the request every time: you lose the cache.

exercicios.texto: List the five tasks you hand off to AI the most and fill in the cost-per-task table with model, on the spot or batch, and fixed start (if you only use a subscription, mark "on the spot").
exercicios.pronto: all five rows have a model and "on the spot" or "batch" marked, with the reason in one sentence.

exercicios.texto: For one week, note the usage of each task: on a subscription, whether you used the larger model and whether you hit the limit; on the API, the amount.
exercicios.pronto: the "usage noted" column is filled in for the whole week.

exercicios.texto: With the week in hand, pick one change (smaller model, batch or fixed start) and test it with the procedure from lesson 6.
exercicios.pronto: the "Decision of the week" line has one tested change, with the result of the comparison.

secoes.sub: AI agent without breaking the bank.
The explanation appears after your answer.

perguntas.p: Sorting 50 emails by topic every week. Which choice makes the most sense?
opcoes: The larger model, just to be safe, since a sorting mistake costs more than the model.
Test it on the smaller model and keep it if it passes the rounds.
Do it by hand so you don't spend anything.
perguntas.explica: A simple, repetitive task usually does well on the smaller model. The multi-round test (lesson 6) tells you whether it can handle it.

perguntas.p: You hit your subscription limit every Thursday. What do you look at first?
opcoes: Whether you need to switch to a pricier plan this very week.
Which task is using the larger model when it doesn't need to.
Whether you can open more free accounts on other tools.
Whether the problem goes away when you delete the project's old conversations.
perguntas.explica: On a subscription, the lever is the right model for each task. The cost-per-task table shows which one is wasting the larger model.

perguntas.p: Who do cache and batch apply to?
opcoes: To those who pay per use through the API; on a subscription, the provider takes care of it.
To everyone who uses ChatGPT, with no setup at all.
Only to those who use the smaller model.
Only to those who work in the terminal.
perguntas.explica: Cache and batch are API features, billed by volume. If you only use a subscription, you take care of the right model and the limit.

itens.texto: Smaller for the simple, middle for everyday, larger for what matters.
A fixed start costs a fraction; what can wait goes in batch at half price.
Usage noted per task, every week, and one tested decision at a time.
